hero.headline: St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware named FSL Pitcher of the Week
hero.teaser: The 22-year-old left-hander struck out 12 batters over seven scoreless innings in two appearances against Fort Myers.
hero.body:
St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware has been named the Florida State League Pitcher of the Week for July 20-26, Minor League Baseball announced Monday.

Ware made two appearances against the Fort Myers Mighty Mussels at Clover Park, starting Tuesday and returning for a relief outing Sunday. The left-hander combined to throw seven scoreless innings, allowing three hits and two walks while striking out 12 batters.

The Mets won both games in which Ware appeared. He earned the victory Sunday after pitching four scoreless innings, allowing one hit and one walk and recording a career-high eight strikeouts as St. Lucie rallied for an 11-8 win.

Ware, 22, was selected by the New York Mets in the 15th round of the 2025 MLB Draft out of LSU. He made his professional debut with St. Lucie in April and has remained with the team throughout the season.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue could lose 116 firefighters if property tax amendment passes
cards.body:
Martin County commissioners are expected to hear a presentation Tuesday outlining how a proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could affect Martin County Fire Rescue if voters approve the constitutional amendment on the November ballot. According to county documents, Martin County Fire Rescue projects it could lose 116 firefighters over the next two years, about one-third of its workforce, because of reduced property tax revenue tied to the proposed amendment.

Martin County Commissioner James Blake Capps said the department has few options to absorb the projected revenue loss because about 93 percent of the Fire Rescue budget is dedicated to personnel. Previous county projections have outlined possible station closures, reductions to specialized teams including HAZMAT, Technical Rescue, the dive team and LifeStar, and delays in replacing equipment. Officials have also warned the proposed cuts could lead to longer emergency response times and affect specialized emergency services provided throughout Martin County.

Capps said a no-overtime policy for all fire rescue personnel would be necessary, which would mean no backfilling of stations with personnel and would result in randomized brownouts of stations. He also warned that if the county shuts down three fire stations, many residents would end up paying higher homeowner's insurance premiums. Residents who live within five miles of a fire station receive a break on homeowner's insurance, but those farther than five miles away pay higher premiums.

No vote on firefighter layoffs or fire station closures is expected during Tuesday's meeting. Instead, commissioners will receive the presentation as they continue evaluating the potential local impacts of the proposed homestead exemption expansion. Voters will have the final say on the constitutional amendment during the November general election. The meeting starts at 9 a.m.

cards.headline: Florida executes two inmates in one day for first time in decades
cards.body:
Florida carried out two executions on Tuesday, putting to death a former police officer in the afternoon and an 80-year-old man in the evening in the first back-to-back executions on a single day in nearly a decade. James Aren Duckett, 68, was pronounced dead at 1:19 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. Duckett was convicted of raping and drowning 11-year-old Teresa McAbee while working as a police officer in central Florida in 1987. He declined to make a final statement. Dominick Anthony Occhicone, 80, was scheduled to be executed at 6 p.m., making him the oldest prisoner executed in Florida's modern history. Occhicone was convicted of killing his ex-girlfriend's parents in 1986.

Governor Ron DeSantis has accelerated the pace of executions over the past 18 months at a rate unseen in Florida since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976, making the state's death chamber the busiest in the nation. Since the beginning of 2025, Florida has carried out nearly half the state executions nationwide. Duckett was the 11th inmate executed by the state this year. If the evening execution proceeded as planned, Florida would have executed 30 people since the beginning of 2025, while the rest of U.S. states combined carried out 35 executions over the same period.

The last time any state executed two inmates on the same day was in Arkansas in April 2017. Florida Department of Corrections records show multiple executions on a single day were more common in the past, with the last occurring on May 12, 1964. Both men had made last-ditch appeals to the U.S. Supreme Court, and the Florida Supreme Court denied their appeals last week. Duckett's attorneys had claimed his innocence and argued the state's handling of DNA evidence produced inconclusive results. Occhicone's attorneys had argued that age-related ailments, including kidney and prostate problems, could make his execution especially painful.

DeSantis oversaw a record 19 executions in 2025, more in a single year than any other Florida governor since the reinstatement of the death penalty. The previous high was eight executions set in 2014. DeSantis has rarely commented on the pace of executions, but previously said his goal is to bring justice to victims families who have waited decades. Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty urged DeSantis to halt both executions, calling the double execution an unprecedented escalation of Florida's use of the death penalty.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Chief warns homestead exemption could force station closures, firefighter layoffs
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli warned Tuesday that a proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could force the closure of three fire stations, lay off 116 firefighters, and eliminate specialized emergency response teams. During the Martin County Commission meeting, Cianciulli presented a planning exercise showing the department's annual budget would decline by $9.5 million in the first year if voters approve the constitutional amendment in November. By the second year, the annual loss would reach $16.5 million, a 22% reduction from the current budget.

Under the scenario, Fire Rescue could close Station 18 on Britt Road, Station 33 in Hobe Sound, and Station 23 on Kanner Highway. The department could be forced to lay off as many as 116 firefighters by the second year, equivalent to one of the department's three shifts. The funding loss could force Martin County to eliminate specialized teams responsible for hazardous materials incidents, technical rescues and dive operations. The department could then have to request assistance from neighboring agencies in Palm Beach or St. Lucie counties, potentially increasing response times.

Cianciulli pointed to the deadly Camp Mystic flooding in Texas as an example of the delays that can occur when a community must rely on outside resources. "They had to call for outside assets, a 14-hour response to start mitigating that scene," Cianciulli said. "We're in a position in the county, if we have any incident here, we are able to do an immediate mitigation. We're not wasting any second." During public comment, one resident and a commissioner questioned whether reducing employee salaries could help address the potential shortfall.

Cianciulli responded that Martin County already has difficulty recruiting trained firefighter-paramedics because departments farther south offer better compensation. "When we did our last class that we had, we had roughly 22 open positions; I only had about three paramedics that actually graduated that class," Cianciulli said. "The rest were firefighter EMTs. It's because the compensation package for a firefighter medic that is already trained is much higher down south." Cianciulli advised residents to learn as much as possible about the proposal and its potential effects before casting their ballots in November.

cards.headline: Mother, grandfather, and girlfriend arrested after 3-month-old dies from dehydration and malnutrition in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: Three people face aggravated manslaughter and child abuse charges after a 3-month-old boy died from dehydration and malnutrition in a Fort Pierce mobile home last August.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriffs Office arrested Nicole Maxwell, her father Robert Maxwell, and his girlfriend Vikki Koon nearly a year after the infant's death. The baby died in August 2025 after living primarily with Robert Maxwell and Koon while his mother lived at her boyfriend's home in Vero Beach. Detective Jennifer Diaz said in her 20 years of law enforcement, this is one of the worst cases she has ever worked.

According to court documents, Koon told deputies she believed a newborn should have two ounces per feeding twice a day. When she ran out of formula, she would fill the bottle with regular milk and add water. An autopsy revealed the infant was emaciated and had a sunken abdomen and widespread lesions consistent with severe dehydration and malnutrition. The medical examiner ruled the death a homicide.

Investigators described the mobile home as extremely hot with a bug infestation, lack of food, and unsafe conditions for walking. A neighbor named Suzan said she had concerns about the children's living conditions and would give two of the boys food and drinks when they knocked on her door. Nicole Maxwell's other children who were living in the mobile home are now in foster care. The case took nearly a year to complete because of the complexity and the need for outside medical experts.

cards.headline: $70 million K-8 school breaks ground in Fort Pierce, will consolidate three St. Lucie County schools
cards.body:
A groundbreaking ceremony marked the start of construction on a new K-8 school in Fort Pierce that will combine three St. Lucie County schools into one facility. The new school will be built on land behind Dan McCarty Middle School and is expected to welcome between 1,500 and 1,800 students when it opens. It will consolidate Dan McCarty Middle, St. Lucie Elementary and Lawnwood Elementary into a single campus.

Superintendent Jon Prince said the project is moving forward on time and on budget. The new facility will feature state-of-the-art technology and serve the north part of St. Lucie County. The decision to consolidate comes as the existing schools show their age. All three were built in the 1950s and 1960s. Dan McCarty Middle Principal Latricia Stubbs-James said some of the things inside the building are antiquated.

The district is funding the $70 million project in part by selling the properties where the three older schools currently stand, offsetting the cost of maintaining aging buildings. Prince said the K-8 model is already proven across the district, which operates 11 other K-8 schools. Attendance is better, test scores are better and grades are better in the K-8s, Prince said. Stubbs-James said the K-8 model offers unique benefits, allowing kindergarten students to see what it looks like to be an eighth grader.

The new Fort Pierce K-8 school is expected to be completed in August 2028.

cards.headline: Man forced to withdraw cash at gunpoint during Wells Fargo ATM robbery in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: Two men forced a customer at a Wells Fargo ATM to withdraw cash at gunpoint Sunday night before fleeing on foot.
cards.body:
A man using a Wells Fargo ATM became the victim of an armed robbery after two men forced him to pull out cash before fleeing the scene on foot Sunday at about 8:38 p.m., according to the Fort Pierce Police Department. One of the men displayed a gun concealed in his waistband before forcing the victim to withdraw an unknown amount of cash.

Officers with the Fort Pierce Police Department responded to the scene, established a perimeter, and used a K-9 and drone to search for the suspects. The suspects were not located. Police described them as two men in their early 20s, about 5 feet 10 inches tall and weighing about 170 pounds. The armed suspect was last seen wearing jeans and a gray hooded sweatshirt.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie police find fleeing suspect hiding on roof of occupied home after high-speed chase
cards.teaser: A suspected drunk driver fled Port St. Lucie police at nearly 80 mph in a 45 mph zone before he and his passenger abandoned their car and ran, with one suspect later found hiding on the roof of an occupied home.
cards.body:
Officers attempted to stop a white Acura after observing multiple traffic violations and signs of impaired driving. Instead of pulling over, the driver accelerated to nearly 80 mph in a 45 mph zone on Southwest Becker Road. Police said the driver and passenger weaved in and out of traffic, ignored traffic signs and signals, then abandoned the vehicle in a residential driveway near Southwest Idol Avenue before fleeing on foot.

A nearby resident called 911 after seeing the two men run from the scene. Police deployed a K-9 and a drone while officers established a perimeter. Both suspects were located, including one who was found hiding on the roof of an occupied home, police said.

The suspects were identified as Joseph Gary Harris, 42, and Bryan Shawn Baker, 46. Harris was charged with fleeing and eluding law enforcement, burglary of an occupied dwelling, resisting an officer without violence, and loitering or prowling. Baker was charged with resisting an officer without violence and loitering or prowling.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County commissioners deadlock on infrastructure tax renewal, postpone decision
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County commissioners split evenly on when to schedule a referendum to renew the county's half-cent infrastructure sales tax, voting unanimously to postpone the decision u
cards.body:
St. Lucie County commissioners split evenly on when to schedule a referendum to renew the county's half-cent infrastructure sales tax, voting unanimously to postpone the decision until August 4. The voter-approved tax expires in December 2028 after its 10-year authorization. Commissioners must decide whether to ask voters to extend it in 2026 or wait until 2028. If they wait and voters approve it then, it would be considered a new tax rather than a continuation.

 Before the commission's discussion on July 21, three Port St. Lucie officials urged the board to place the referendum on the 2026 ballot. Port St. Lucie Public Works Director Colt Schwerdt said the tax has funded road, sidewalk, stormwater and water-quality improvements that have benefited city residents. Utility Systems Director Kevin Matyjaszek said there is a direct correlation between infrastructure and quality of life. Communications Director Sarah Prohaska read a letter from Kenneth Kroll, chairman of both the county and Port St. Lucie Sales Tax Oversight committees, who urged commissioners to act this year.

 Commissioner James Clasby opposed placing the measure on the 2026 ballot, saying he did not want it on the same ballot as Amendment 3 and the School Board tax. Commissioner Erin Lowry agreed, saying many residents are struggling financially and may reject the measure simply because it includes the word tax. Chairwoman Jamie Fowler argued the county would have two opportunities if the measure were placed on the 2026 ballot. Commissioner Cathy Townsend agreed and moved to keep the referendum on the 2026 ballot, but the motion failed on a 2-2 vote.

 With Vice Chairman Larry Leet absent and the commission deadlocked, members voted 4-0 to continue the item until August 4, when Leet is expected to return and cast the deciding vote. Deputy County Administrator Mayte Santamaria reminded commissioners they had already approved an ordinance in March scheduling the referendum for November 2026. Keeping that date requires no action, while delaying it until 2028 would require rescinding the ordinance and adopting a new one.

cards.headline: Indiantown Village Council rejects second attempt at data center pause
cards.teaser: Two Indiantown Village Council members failed to convince colleagues to approve a pause on data center applications, with the village attorney warning the move would violate state legislation.
cards.body:
Indiantown Village Councilwoman Karen Onsager moved that the Village of Indiantown establish a 90-day administrative pause on the acceptance, processing and approval of all new applications for large-load data center development projects during the July 13 budget workshop. The motion died after no council member offered a second. Onsager had requested the pause to allow the council and residents to better understand current and projected demands on water and electrical infrastructure through an informational meeting with technical experts, representatives from the South Florida Water Management District and utility providers.

 Village Attorney Wade Vose said such an administrative pause, whether 90 days or 12 months, would violate Senate Bill 180. Vose said he received an email that same afternoon from a local land use attorney who represents multiple developers within the Village, warning that SB 180 would prohibit anything along the lines of a regulation that would inhibit the process of applications for development. Mayor Carmine Dipaolo warned colleagues about offending state officials who have given the village over $120 million in funding.

 The council previously sought advice from Vose last month on a moratorium after scores of local residents protested the village's preliminary review of a data center application submitted by Nelson Ferreira, which he withdrew on April 29. Village Manager Taryn Kryzda confirmed the industrially zoned lands within the village allowed data centers as a permitted use. Onsager confirmed with Kryzda that a community meeting would be scheduled for Saturday, Aug. 2.

cards.headline: Cyclist rides through Vero Beach on 2,600-mile journey from Key West to Maine
cards.teaser: A Boston cyclist rode through Vero Beach this week on a 2,600-mile bike ride from Key West to Maine to honor a friend lost to colorectal cancer.
cards.body:
Jay Weedall traveled to South Florida to begin the journey, with a goal of raising $50,000 for the Young Onset Colorectal Cancer Research Center. Weedall began his journey in Key West, pedaling 155 miles to Miami on day one. He set off on his second leg, a 163-mile ride to Vero Beach, after filling his hydration pack with ice to stay cool.

 Weedall is riding roughly 150 miles a day up the coast through nearly every state all the way to the Pan Mass Challenge. He will do the Pan Mass Challenge across Massachusetts on August 2 and continue to the Canadian border in Maine. By avoiding highways, Weedall says the route offers something unexpected, allowing him to experience little coastal towns along the inlets. Fans can follow Weedall's journey on the cycling app Strava.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie cuts property tax rate for 11th straight year
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie City Council lowered the city's millage rate to 4.8750 for fiscal year 2026-27, down from 4.9750, continuing an 11-year trend of property tax reductions.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council agreed to lower the city's property tax millage rate for the 11th consecutive year at the annual Summer Workshop held July 22-23. The Council approved a millage rate of 4.8750 for fiscal year 2026-27, a decrease from 4.9750 in fiscal year 2025-26. The budget will be adopted by City Council in September, with public hearings taking place Sept. 4 and Sept. 18, and goes into effect Oct. 1.

 Since 2016, the city has reduced its millage rate by 25 percent, saving the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over a 10-year period. Port St. Lucie has the third lowest municipal tax rate out of Florida's 20 largest cities. The property tax reduction maintains Port St. Lucie's record of steadily reducing its millage rate while managing historic population growth, investing in essential infrastructure and improving public safety.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie opens $28.8 million police training center with 20-lane indoor firing range
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie cut the ribbon on a three-story, 54,283-square-foot police training facility on the City Hall grounds featuring advanced virtual reality technology and indoor firearms capabilities.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie officially opened its $28.8 million police training center on July 24 with a ribbon-cutting ceremony on the City Hall grounds just northwest of the police department. The 54,283-square-foot, three-story facility was four years in construction and was designed by ADG Architecture and built by HJ High. Mayor Shannon Martin said the project ensures officers have the space, training, and resources needed to serve the community at the highest level.

 The facility includes a 20-lane, 9,508-square-foot indoor firearms range with an integrated MILO live-fire scenario system, a 2,848-square-foot tactical shoot house with configurable rooms, and a MILO Virtual Simulation Theater for decision-making and de-escalation exercises. It also features a defensive tactics training room equipped with Axon VR technology, a multi-purpose training room, and three floors of office space supporting the Training Division and Criminal Investigations Division with 19 offices and 86 workstations.

 Officer Brittany McNally said the facility will reduce recurring costs from officers traveling to Indian River State College in Fort Pierce for training. The new training center provides access to state-of-the-art technology and realistic scenario-based training that better prepares officers for situations they may face in the field, she said. Police personnel immediately began moving into the facility after the ribbon cutting. The facility is not open to the general public due to safety and confidentiality concerns.

hero.headline: Three arrested in Fort Pierce after 3-month-old dies from dehydration and malnutrition in 'one of the worst cases'
hero.body:
Three people face charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse after a 3-month-old died from dehydration and malnutrition in a Fort Pierce mobile home, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. Nicole Maxwell, the infant's mother, her father Robert Maxwell, and his girlfriend Vikki Koon were arrested nearly a year after the child's death in August 2025. Detective Jennifer Diaz called it one of the worst cases in her 20 years of law enforcement.

The investigation began when Robert Maxwell and Koon brought the infant to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital already deceased on Aug. 20, 2025. The medical examiner determined the child died from dehydration and malnutrition and ruled the death a homicide. Court documents describe the infant's ribs as more prominent than its stomach. The child had lived primarily with Robert Maxwell and Koon in a mobile home in the 800 block of Silverstream Circle in Fort Pierce while Nicole Maxwell lived with her boyfriend in Vero Beach. The child's father lives in Virginia.

Investigators described the mobile home as having windows boarded shut, exposed electrical wiring, and live and dead cockroaches throughout. Koon told investigators she fed the infant only twice a day and when she ran out of formula, she gave the child watered-down milk with baby cereal mixed in. A neighbor named Suzan said she witnessed the conditions firsthand and would see other children from the home asking for water. The house was extremely hot with a bug infestation, a lack of food, and was unsafe for walking, according to Diaz.

Nicole Maxwell's four other children, ranging in age from 2 to 10 years old, were living in the mobile home and have been placed in foster care through the Department of Children and Families. Koon and Robert Maxwell are in the St. Lucie County Jail each on $1.5 million bond. Nicole Maxwell was arrested July 23 at a home in the 300 block of 12th Street SW in Vero Beach and is being held in the Indian River County Jail on no bond. Diaz said DCF had been involved with the family before and urged residents to report suspicious activity to protect children.

cards.body:
Indian River County Fire Rescue is mourning the loss of Firefighter and Paramedic Geoffrey Lang, who died while off duty Saturday night. The department announced his passing in a statement and asked the community to keep his loved ones in their thoughts.

Suzan, who lives across the street from the mobile home in the 800 block of Silverstream Circle in Fort Pierce, said she had concerns about the children's living conditions and believes the arrests are long overdue. She said two of the boys would knock on her door and she would give them food and something to drink. Suzan said sheets of plywood covered holes in the mobile home's floor and she had been inside the house, which she described as unlivable.

St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro released a statement following the arrests reminding the public that protecting children is a responsibility everyone shares. He said if residents see signs that a child may be neglected, abused, or living in unsafe conditions, they should not assume someone else will intervene. One phone call can be the difference between a child receiving the help they need and a life being saved, according to Del Toro.

cards.headline: St. Lucie detective describes conditions in Fort Pierce mobile home where infant died
cards.teaser: Detective Jennifer Diaz said the Fort Pierce mobile home where a 3-month-old died was extremely hot with a bug infestation and lacked safe entry.
cards.body:

The house was extremely hot, there was a bug infestation in the home, a lack of food, and the home was unsafe for walking, she said during a July 27 press briefing. There was not an entry way that investigators could safely make entry into.

Diaz said it took nearly a year for charges to be brought against the caregivers because it was a very complicated investigation. With the death of a child, investigators had to seek out outside experts, which can take several weeks or even months. In questioning the biological mother, Diaz said the woman showed a lack of emotion and lack of empathy to the child. Diaz, the biological mother of two and the foster mother of 11, said the case was very hard and the way the child ended their last days of life was very sad for her.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County school district cuts 19 workers as Temporary Protected Status expires
hero.teaser: The Palm Beach County School District is separating 19 employees from employment today as Temporary Protected Status expires for Haitian workers.
hero.body:
The School District of Palm Beach County confirmed 19 district employees will be separated from employment as all school district employees must be legally authorized to work in the United States. Chuck Ridley, director of civic engagement for the Service Employees International Union, said the union expects hundreds of workers statewide to be affected, with nearly 20 employees in the Palm Beach County School District alone.

Ridley said many of the workers losing TPS protections are bus drivers, custodians, paraprofessionals, food service employees and city workers. He warned that without drivers to pick up students or workers to provide public services, residents will see disruptions in schools, garbage collection and other city functions. The healthcare system could also face staffing shortages, particularly in hospitals and nursing homes that rely heavily on immigrant workers.

The Florida Healthcare Association said Haitian caregivers are valued members of the long term care workforce, serving as certified nursing assistants, nurses, dietary aides, housekeepers and other essential team members. The association said a disruption to experienced staff could create additional challenges to long term care centers focused on supporting the needs of residents, families and care teams. According to the Lar Management Group, the Haitian community contributes an estimated $1.2 billion to Florida's economy.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie bans gas station on Tradition commercial site after months of resident concerns
cards.teaser: The Port St.
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council has permanently prohibited a gas station from being built on a 9.4-acre commercial parcel at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Drive. The council unanimously approved the 16th amendment to the Tradition Master Planned Unit Development on July 13, ending months of debate over converting what had been planned as Phase 3 of the Heritage Oaks at Tradition residential development into commercial property.

The amendment changes the parcel designation from residential to commercial, allowing retail and office development while addressing resident concerns about traffic and congestion along Crosstown Parkway west of Interstate 95. The restriction bars any current or future owner from developing a service station on the site, with the prohibition now written directly into the Tradition MPUD documents. City planner Bridget Kean confirmed the restriction will remain with the property regardless of ownership.

The issue began nearly three months earlier when Winding River Crosstown LLC requested permission to convert the residential site to commercial use. During the initial May 26 hearing, Vice Mayor Jolien Caraballo and other council members voiced concerns that a convenience store with gas pumps would worsen traffic in the rapidly growing area. The council tabled the request to allow staff time to determine whether gas stations could be eliminated as a permitted use.

Before any construction begins, the developer must install a fence along the southern property line to prevent construction access through Southwest Glenbrook Drive, which connects to Heritage Oaks. An architectural wall and landscape buffering must be completed along the southeastern and southern boundaries before the first building permit is issued for vertical construction. Councilman Anthony Bonna defended the decision, saying expanding commercial development will benefit residents by broadening the city's tax base. Councilman David Pickett said going to commercial is the best possible outcome for that corner.

cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved the final reading of an amendment July 13 that permanently prohibits a gas station from being built on a 9.4-acre commercial parcel at the southwest corner of Crosstown Parkway and Fairgreen Drive in Tradition. The council vote codifies a restriction that bars any current or future owner from developing a service station on the site, ending nearly three months of debate. The amendment changes the parcel designation from residential to commercial, paving the way for retail and office development while addressing residents' concerns about traffic and congestion.

 The issue began when Winding River Crosstown LLC requested permission to convert what had been planned as Phase 3 of the Heritage Oaks at Tradition residential development into commercial property. Vice Mayor Jolien Caraballo and other council members noted the increasing congestion along the commercial corridor and asked staff to determine whether gas stations could be eliminated as a permitted use on the parcel.

 The council tabled the request at a May 26 hearing to allow time for that review. Several Heritage Oaks residents urged the council at a June 22 hearing to reject the land-use change, citing concerns about increased traffic, noise and neighborhood impacts. Instead, the council voted 4-0, with Councilwoman Stephanie Morgan absent, to approve the commercial designation on first reading after the developer agreed to permanently relinquish the right to build a gas station.

 City planner Bridget Kean outlined the changes that formally incorporated the restriction into the Tradition Master Planned Unit Development documents at the July 13 meeting. The updated development plan specifies that while service stations remain a permitted use elsewhere within the mixed-use area, they are prohibited on Parcel 11A. Staff also added additional protections requested by nearby residents.

 Before any mass grading begins, the developer must install a fence along the southern property line to prevent construction access through Southwest Glenbrook Drive, which connects to Heritage Oaks. An architectural wall and landscape buffering must be completed along the southeastern and southern boundaries before the first building permit is issued for vertical construction.

 Councilman Anthony Bonna defended both the public process and the final compromise, saying the city has consistently heard residents oppose additional housing. Councilman David Pickett said going to commercial is the best possible thing for that corner. Mayor Shannon Martin asked staff to confirm that the prohibition would remain with the property regardless of ownership.

 Kean confirmed the restriction is now written directly into the Tradition MPUD documents, ensuring no future owner can develop a gas station on the parcel. The council then voted unanimously to approve the ordinance.

cards.headline: TPS expiration leaves Haitian workers in Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce without jobs
cards.teaser: Temporary Protected Status expired Monday for Haitian immigrants, stripping workers of jobs and disrupting schools and public services across the Treasure Coast.
cards.body:
Valentina Lorissaint said many relatives and friends are already unable to work after losing authorization tied to TPS. She said a lot of people have been scared, just wondering what the next meal they're going to eat the next day. Residents described widespread anxiety rippling through the community, with some families afraid to leave their homes or send children to school.

 Chuck Ridley, director of civic engagement for the Service Employees International Union, said the union expects hundreds of workers statewide to be affected, including nearly 20 employees in the Palm Beach County School District alone. The Palm Beach County School District said 19 District employees will be separated from employment as all School District employees must be legally authorized to work in the United States. Ridley said many of the workers losing TPS protections are bus drivers, custodians, paraprofessionals, food service employees and city workers.

 The Florida Healthcare Association said Haitian caregivers are valued members of the long term care workforce, serving as certified nursing assistants, nurses, dietary aides, housekeepers and other essential team members. According to the Lar Management Group, the Haitian community contributes an estimated $1.2 billion to Florida's economy. TPS allows people from countries facing war, natural disasters or other unsafe conditions to live and work temporarily in the United States. The U.S. State Department currently maintains a Level 4 Do Not Travel advisory for Haiti, citing crime, civil unrest and kidnapping.

cards.headline: Treasure Coast single-family home prices rise after two-year decline
cards.teaser: Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after drops from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St.
cards.body:
Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after drops from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000.

 Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down. Inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers.

 Cara Collins, who bought her Martin County home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell. Collins said current prices are higher than she would hope for, and that the market has changed what would be possible for her family today. She said she would not be able to be a stay-at-home mom and be able to afford a home for her kids if buying now.

 Condos and townhomes show different trends. Prices have dropped in Martin and St. Lucie counties and only increased by less than a percent in Indian River County. Decowski said buyers need to come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes, and sellers need to price their homes realistically and present a well-maintained product.

cards.headline: Private racetrack resort community breaks ground in St. Lucie County on 650 acres
cards.teaser: P1 Motor Club is under construction on 650 acres off Okeechobee Road in St. Lucie County, replacing fairways with racing circuits and preparing to welcome its first drivers this fa
cards.body:
P1 Motor Club is under construction on 650 acres off Okeechobee Road in St. Lucie County, replacing fairways with racing circuits and preparing to welcome its first drivers this fall. The private racetrack resort community features 10 miles of racing circuits designed for street cars, race cars and go-karts. Chris DuPlessis, Director of Fun for P1 Motor Club, compared the concept to a high-end golf resort, except with a racetrack instead of a golf course.

 The first track under construction is the 3-mile Treasure Coast Track, set to open in October. Over the next six months, crews will continue work on additional circuits, including the flagship 4.5-mile P1 International Circuit. DuPlessis said the club is designed for drivers of all ages and skill levels, with kids as young as 8 years old driving go-karts all the way up to grandparents still driving their cars on track, making it a family club.

 Membership comes with a $192,000 initiation fee and $12,000 in yearly dues. The club already has 260 members. Construction on a clubhouse and homes for up to 125 residents is scheduled to begin in 2027. The development will also include condos and customizable garages with living spaces situated directly along the tracks.

 Despite the scale of the project, developers say they want to preserve the character of the region by planting trees, creating lakes, and incorporating natural landscaping throughout the property. DuPlessis said it will feel like the racetrack has been there for 100 years, comparing the scope of work to building a city. P1 Motor Club is expected to be fully completed by 2028.

cards.headline: Survey finds 64% say inflation made basics harder to afford, 42% skipped medical care
cards.teaser: A 2026 survey from eHealth found 64% of those polled say inflation has made it harder to afford basics like food, housing and clothing, with 42% saying they skipped or delayed medical care in the past year.
cards.body:
A 2026 survey from eHealth found 64% of those polled say inflation has made it harder to afford basics like food, housing and clothing, forcing many Americans to make difficult choices between necessities like rent, groceries and healthcare. The study reveals that healthcare is often losing out when people are forced to prioritize their spending.

 Medicare recipients are especially finding it challenging to afford healthcare amid rising costs. Judith Waseka, who attended a Let's Hear It community event in Vero Beach, said even with supplemental help, she and her husband are having a hard time affording their prescription drugs. "You either eat or you pay for your medication, or you sell your house or you pay for your medication," Waseka said.

 The financial pressures are leading to serious consequences for people's health. Forty-two percent of those polled say they've skipped or delayed medical care in the past year because of inflation, according to the eHealth study. This means nearly half of respondents are going without needed medical attention due to cost concerns.

 The survey highlights how inflation is forcing Americans to make impossible choices between basic necessities. When stretched budgets cannot cover housing, food and medical care simultaneously, many are choosing to forgo healthcare rather than go without shelter or meals. The findings underscore the growing financial strain facing families, particularly those on Medicare who are living on fixed incomes while trying to manage healthcare expenses that continue to rise.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware named FSL Pitcher of the Week
hero.teaser: The 22-year-old left-hander struck out 12 batters over seven scoreless innings in two appearances against Fort Myers.
hero.body:
St. Lucie Mets pitcher Conner Ware has been named the Florida State League Pitcher of the Week for July 20-26, Minor League Baseball announced Monday.

Ware made two appearances against the Fort Myers Mighty Mussels at Clover Park, starting Tuesday and returning for a relief outing Sunday. The left-hander combined to throw seven scoreless innings, allowing three hits and two walks while striking out 12 batters.

The Mets won both games in which Ware appeared. He earned the victory Sunday after pitching four scoreless innings, allowing one hit and one walk and recording a career-high eight strikeouts as St. Lucie rallied for an 11-8 win.

Ware, 22, was selected by the New York Mets in the 15th round of the 2025 MLB Draft out of LSU. He made his professional debut with St. Lucie in April and has remained with the team throughout the season.

cards.headline: Mets erase 5-0 deficit to beat Mighty Mussels 11-8
cards.teaser: Jeremy Rodriguez went 4-for-4, and Conner Ware struck out a career-high eight as St. Lucie scored eight runs in the second inning.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie Mets erased an early five-run deficit with an eight-run second inning and rallied for an 11-8 win over the Fort Myers Mighty Mussels on Sunday afternoon at Clover Park.

 Fort Myers won the seven-game series 4-3 and finished the season series with an 8-4 advantage.

 The Mighty Mussels scored three runs in the first inning and two more in the second to build a 5-0 lead. St. Lucie responded with eight runs in the bottom of the second and moved ahead for good.

 Randy Guzman delivered the decisive hit, lining a two-out, two-run single that turned a 5-4 deficit into a 6-5 Mets lead. Julio Zayas followed with a two-run single to extend the advantage to 8-5.

 The Mets added three runs in the third. Elian Peña hit an RBI single, Jacob Reimer drove in a run with a double and Trey Snyder added a sacrifice fly to make it 11-5.

 Conner Ware took over on the mound in the third inning and settled the game down for St. Lucie. Ware pitched four scoreless innings, allowed one hit and one walk, and struck out a career-high eight batters. He struck out the side swinging in the fourth and struck out the side looking in the sixth before earning the win.

 Fort Myers scored three runs in the seventh against Luis Sotillo, who was making his Mets debut. Sotillo recovered by retiring six of the final seven batters he faced and carried the game through the eighth inning.

 Elwis Mijares worked a perfect ninth on six pitches to record his third save.

 Jeremy Rodriguez led the Mets at the plate, going 4-for-4 with a double, an RBI and two runs scored from the No. 9 spot in the order. Zayas and Peña collected two hits apiece.

 Reimer, beginning a minor league rehabilitation assignment for a groin injury, went 1-for-3 with a double, a walk, two RBIs and two runs scored. He played all nine innings at third base.

 The Mets improved to 11-18 in the second half and 44-51 overall. They are off Monday before opening a six-game road series against the Dunedin Blue Jays on Tuesday. First pitch at TD Ballpark is scheduled for 6:30 p.m.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Mets Fall Short in 15-14 Loss to Fort Myers
cards.teaser: Randy Guzman hit two home runs and drove in six as the St. Lucie Mets nearly erased an eight-run deficit in a 15-14 loss to Fort Myers.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie Mets nearly erased an eight-run first-inning deficit but fell one run short in a 15-14 loss to the Fort Myers Mighty Mussels on Saturday night at Clover Park.

 Fort Myers scored eight runs in the opening inning and survived several St. Lucie rallies to earn its third consecutive victory.

 Mets starter Ethan Lanthier was charged with seven runs on five hits and two walks before being removed with two outs in the first inning. Harry Genth delivered a three-run double during the Mussels' early outburst.

 Mets Answer With Five-Run First Inning

 St. Lucie immediately responded with five runs against Fort Myers starter Matt Barr in the bottom of the first. Antonio Jimenez, Branny De Oleo and Simon Juan each recorded RBI hits to cut the deficit to 8-5.

 The Mighty Mussels added three runs against Franyel Diaz in the third inning. Ramiro Dominguez drove in two with a single, and Byron Chourio hit a solo home run to extend the Fort Myers lead to 11-5.

 Trey Snyder helped St. Lucie pull closer in the fourth inning with an unconventional trip around the bases. Snyder's ground-ball single was mishandled by shortstop Quetin Young, who then committed a throwing error that allowed Snyder to score and another run to cross the plate.

 The play cut the Mussels' lead to 11-7.

 Guzman Homers Twice

 Randy Guzman hit a two-run homer against Ramiro Villanueva in the fifth inning to bring the Mets within two runs.

 Villanueva later hit consecutive batters and was ejected. St. Lucie loaded the bases with one out, but reliever Adam Falinski retired Elian Pena on a popout and Snyder on a groundout to preserve the 11-9 Fort Myers advantage.

 Young answered with a three-run home run over the batter's eye in the sixth, pushing the Mussels' lead to 14-9.

 Guzman responded again in the bottom half of the inning, launching a three-run homer to make it 14-12.

 He finished the game 3-for-4 with two home runs, a single, six RBIs and two runs scored.

 Ninth-Inning Rally Falls One Run Short

 Ricardo Paez opened the ninth inning with a solo home run that gave Fort Myers a 15-13 lead and provided what proved to be a crucial insurance run.

 Francisco Toledo scored on a wild pitch and throwing error with one out in the bottom of the ninth. Marco Vargas then homered to right field with two outs, pulling St. Lucie within one run at 15-14.

 Brent Francisco struck out Chase Meggers to end the game and record his third save.

 Michael Hilker Jr. earned the win after pitching 2 1/3 scoreless innings of relief for Fort Myers. Lanthier took the loss.

 Jimenez went 2-for-3 with two walks and three runs scored. Vargas, De Oleo and Juan added two hits apiece.

 The Mets fell to 10-18 in the second half and 43-51 overall. The Mighty Mussels improved to 14-14 in the second half and 51-42 overall.

 The teams will conclude their series Sunday at Clover Park. First pitch is scheduled for 12:10 p.m.

cards.headline: Zayas Homers Twice as St. Lucie Mets Cruise Past Mighty Mussels
cards.teaser:
Julio Zayas homered twice and Trey Snyder continued his hot stretch at the plate as the St. Lucie Mets defeated the Fort Myers Mighty Mussels 8-2 Tuesday night at Clover Park.

The
cards.body:
Julio Zayas homered twice and Trey Snyder continued his hot stretch at the plate as the St. Lucie Mets defeated the Fort Myers Mighty Mussels 8-2 Tuesday night at Clover Park.

The victory in the series opener was St. Lucie's fifth win in its last six games.

The Mets held a 1-0 lead through two innings before breaking the game open with four runs against Fort Myers starter Eric Hammond in the third.

Randy Guzman drew a bases-loaded walk to bring home the first run of the inning. Snyder followed with a two-run double before scoring on a throwing error after Antonio Jimenez singled, extending the Mets' lead to 5-0.

Jimenez added a sacrifice fly in the fifth inning to make it 6-0.

Zayas provided the rest of St. Lucie's offense with solo home runs in the sixth and eighth innings. He became the second Mets player this season to record a multi-homer game, joining Guzman.

Zayas finished 3-for-4 with his fifth and sixth home runs of the season.

Snyder also went 3-for-3 with a double, a walk, two RBIs and a run scored. He has collected seven hits over his last two games.

St. Lucie starter Conner Ware pitched three scoreless innings, allowing no runs while striking out four.

Emilio Obispo earned the win after allowing two runs on two hits over four innings. He walked three and struck out three.

Zack Mack pitched a scoreless eighth inning before Elwis Mijares worked the ninth and induced a 4-6-3 double play to end the game.

The Mets improved to 9-14 in the second half and 42-47 overall. The Mighty Mussels fell to 10-13 in the second half and 47-41 overall.

The teams will play the second game of the series Wednesday at Clover Park. The Mets will hold their annual Summer Camp Day, with first pitch scheduled for 11:10 a.m.

cards.headline: Messi bathed Yamal as baby in 2007 photo shoot, now they meet in World Cup final
cards.teaser: A 2007 charity calendar photo shoot paired teenage Lionel Messi with infant Lamine Yamal. Now 19 years later, they face off in Sunday's World Cup final.
cards.body:
Photographer Joan Monfort took photos in 2007 of a teenage Lionel Messi bathing infant Lamine Yamal in a plastic bathtub as part of a charity calendar produced by local newspaper Sport and UNICEF. Monfort, who works as a freelance photojournalist for The Associated Press, took the photos after Yamal's mother won a raffle of families in the city of Mataró near Barcelona who wanted to participate.

 Soccer destiny paired her baby boy with the Argentine who would become the greatest of all time. Messi left Barcelona in 2021 when the club was in financial trouble. Yamal erupted at the club two years later.

 Monfort had no recollection of the photos until Yamal's father posted one on social media during the 2024 European Championship, when a teenage Yamal led Spain to the title. The photo went viral then, but interest has skyrocketed with Sunday's World Cup final between Argentina and Spain approaching. Monfort said he has been bombarded by queries for the photos by professional media outlets while also seeing his images reproduced countless times on social media and the internet without any credit or compensation.

 The 19-year-old Yamal will face a Messi who is 20 years his senior in Sunday's final. Monfort, 58, is considering traveling to see the final in New Jersey. He said his heart is split and he does not know if he wants Messi or Yamal to win.

cards.headline: President Trump to Attend World Cup Final in New Jersey with Stepped-Up Security
cards.teaser: The World Cup final Sunday in New Jersey has been designated a Level 1 Special Event with President Trump attending the trophy presentation and enhanced security from multiple federal agencies.
cards.body:
The 2026 FIFA World Cup began with 48 teams playing over 39 days. Now it comes down to one final match Sunday in New Jersey. As Argentina and Spain prepare to take the pitch, a sprawling network of federal agents, local law enforcement, and private companies continue with a game plan two years in the making to ensure the final is safe.

 A joint operations center in New York has helped oversee security and monitor threats in host cities throughout the tournament, with thousands of personnel on the ground and a team with an eye on the skies. The FBI has seized hundreds of drones flying in restricted airspace near stadiums during the tournament.

 The final will include a beefed-up Secret Service perimeter, with President Trump attending the trophy presentation. White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt says his attendance will cap what has been the most watched, most secure, and most successful World Cup in American history. When Trump attended an NBA Finals game last month in New York, police shut down several city blocks around the arena and fans were forced to wait in extra-long lines to go through enhanced security.

 The World Cup final is a Level 1 Special Event, the highest possible security designation, with added resources from the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Defense, and the FBI. No one will be allowed to simply walk up to the stadium or drive a personal vehicle.

Coastal Connections will lead an activity in the Laura and Bill Buck Atrium where visitors can make friendship bracelets using recycled fishing line collected from local waterways. Participants can also learn about the organization's Fishing Line Recycling Program.

The museum has adopted the fishing line recycling tube at the Riverside Park boat ramp. From 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., families can take short, docent-led gallery tours through the Museum Studios family program. Visitors can then participate in Nature in Layers, an art activity for children connected to the museum's exhibitions.

Guests can also tour the museum's summer exhibitions throughout the day. James Prosek: At Work is on view in the Holmes Gallery, while Jill Nathanson: Chromatic Phrases is displayed in the Schumann and Titelman galleries. Second Saturday includes free museum admission throughout the day.

Kendra Bergman, founder and executive director of Coastal Connections, said the partnership is an example of how the organization is working with the community to introduce everyone to marine conservation and environmental protection in unique ways. Coastal Connections was founded in 2017 with a mission of advancing the survival of sea turtles by educating and connecting people to the environment.

hero.headline: Florida executes two inmates in one day for first time in decades
hero.body:
Florida carried out two executions on Tuesday, putting to death a former police officer in the afternoon and an 80-year-old man in the evening in the first back-to-back executions on a single day in nearly a decade. James Aren Duckett, 68, was pronounced dead at 1:19 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. Duckett was convicted of raping and drowning 11-year-old Teresa McAbee while working as a police officer in central Florida in 1987. He declined to make a final statement. Dominick Anthony Occhicone, 80, was scheduled to be executed at 6 p.m., making him the oldest prisoner executed in Florida's modern history. Occhicone was convicted of killing his ex-girlfriend's parents in 1986.

Governor Ron DeSantis has accelerated the pace of executions over the past 18 months at a rate unseen in Florida since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976, making the state's death chamber the busiest in the nation. Since the beginning of 2025, Florida has carried out nearly half the state executions nationwide. Duckett was the 11th inmate executed by the state this year. If the evening execution proceeded as planned, Florida would have executed 30 people since the beginning of 2025, while the rest of U.S. states combined carried out 35 executions over the same period.

The last time any state executed two inmates on the same day was in Arkansas in April 2017. Florida Department of Corrections records show multiple executions on a single day were more common in the past, with the last occurring on May 12, 1964. Both men had made last-ditch appeals to the U.S. Supreme Court, and the Florida Supreme Court denied their appeals last week. Duckett's attorneys had claimed his innocence and argued the state's handling of DNA evidence produced inconclusive results. Occhicone's attorneys had argued that age-related ailments, including kidney and prostate problems, could make his execution especially painful.

DeSantis oversaw a record 19 executions in 2025, more in a single year than any other Florida governor since the reinstatement of the death penalty. The previous high was eight executions set in 2014. DeSantis has rarely commented on the pace of executions, but previously said his goal is to bring justice to victims families who have waited decades. Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty urged DeSantis to halt both executions, calling the double execution an unprecedented escalation of Florida's use of the death penalty.

cards.headline: Poll shows Florida property tax amendment support depends on how voters are informed
cards.teaser: A University of North Florida poll found 61 percent support for Florida's proposed property tax amendment initially, but support fell to 45 percent after voters learned of an estimated $11.8 billion municipal budget shortfall.
cards.body:
A new poll showed Florida's proposed property tax amendment may be popular enough to pass depending on how it is described to voters. The proposal would raise the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes from $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and then to $250,000 in 2028. It would also lower the annual assessment growth cap for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent and restrict how local governments spend remaining property tax revenue.

 The UNF survey initially found 61 percent support after respondents were told the amendment would reserve property tax revenue for core public services. That is narrowly above the 60 percent approval required for a constitutional amendment. Support fell 16 points, however, after respondents were told the proposal is estimated to create an approximately $11.8 billion municipal budget shortfall over two years.

 With that information, 45 percent supported the amendment and 47 percent opposed it. The poll surveyed 848 likely midterm voters from July 8 through July 17.

 Those results add significance to three lawsuits challenging the amendment's ballot title and summary. Plaintiffs argue phrases promising to protect small businesses, ensure fairness and preserve core services amount to political advertising instead of a neutral description of the proposal. The challengers are not asking a judge to remove the amendment from the November ballot.

 If the language is found defective, state law would require Attorney General James Uthmeier to rewrite what voters see. A hearing on the ballot language challenges is scheduled for July 29 in Leon County.

cards.headline: Jellyfish Museum in Pompano Beach showcases medical breakthroughs from ancient sea creatures
cards.teaser: Researchers at the Jellyfish Museum in Pompano Beach have developed an antidote for the potentially fatal sting of the box jellyfish. Other medical advances include collagen harvested from flame jellies that has been found to help stop hemorrhages.
cards.body:
The Jellyfish Museum in Pompano Beach houses thousands of jellyfish in all sizes and shapes, offering a window into some of the ocean's most ethereal and elusive creatures. Naphtalie Jeanty, who holds degrees in both archaeology and anthropology, found her way to the museum through a passion for teaching about flora and fauna. Jellyfish have been gracefully moving through the world's oceans for over 500 million years, making them some of the oldest living species on Earth, predating dinosaurs, trees and even fish.

 Despite the name, jellyfish are not technically fish at all. Jeanty said a lot of the world is starting to describe them as just jellies, and they do not have the same anatomy as fish.

 Researchers at the museum have developed an antidote for the potentially fatal sting of the box jellyfish, which can kill its prey in 3 to 5 minutes. Jeanty said she thinks it is going to be a breakthrough. Other medical advances involve collagen harvested from flame jellies.

 The collagen has been apparently found to help stop hemorrhages, so it might be found in bandages in the future. Research into the Japanese sea nettle has also yielded promising results. There is a part of them that was found to shrink tumors in a mouse cancer, and the next step would be possibly human cancer.

 Jellyfish also perform something called symmetrization, the ability to reorganize their bodies for balance. Moon jellies can regenerate after being split in half, creating two different versions of themselves. Some jellyfish even scrub out microplastics, among the smallest particles of pollution found in seas.

 Polka dotted jellies on display at the museum are native to a lake on the island of Palau in the South Pacific, where they work to keep the lake alive. Jeanty said they provide nutrients and move nutrients all throughout the ocean, taking out excess ones that do not need to be there.

cards.headline: Leon County judge rules James Fishback can remain on Florida governor ballot
cards.teaser: Republican gubernatorial candidate James Fishback will remain on Florida's Aug. 18 primary ballot after a Leon County judge rejected Lt. Gov. Jay Collins' challenge to his residenc
cards.body:
Republican gubernatorial candidate James Fishback will remain on Florida's Aug. 18 primary ballot after a Leon County judge rejected Lt. Gov. Jay Collins' challenge to his residency qualifications. Circuit Judge David Frank ruled Monday that Collins did not present enough evidence to overcome Florida's legal presumptions favoring continued residency and candidate access to the ballot.

 The final order denies Collins' request to remove Fishback, declares that the Department of State properly certified his candidacy and says Fishback shall remain qualified for the Republican nomination for governor. Collins sued Fishback in June, arguing the candidate failed to meet the Florida Constitution's requirement that a governor reside in the state for the seven years preceding the election.

 During an expedited hearing last week, Collins' attorneys presented voter registration, mortgage, tax and homestead records they argued showed Fishback established legal residency in Washington, D.C., between 2019 and 2022. Fishback voted in Washington during the 2020 presidential election, filed D.C. resident income tax returns and signed mortgage paperwork describing a condominium there as his principal residence.

 Frank acknowledged those records could carry consequences outside the Florida candidacy case, writing that the various election and financial filings could result in regulatory or more severe legal repercussions for Fishback under Washington, D.C. law. But the judge found they did not prove Fishback intended to abandon Florida as his permanent home. Fishback testified for several hours that he never intended to move his legal domicile from Florida.

 He acknowledged signing mortgage paperwork identifying the Washington condominium as his primary residence but said he rushed through the documents without reading them closely. He also characterized his 2020 D.C. vote as an inadvertent registration during the pandemic, saying he was staying with his parents and wanted to vote for President Donald Trump.

 Frank found Fishback credible on the central issue of intent. The judge also pointed to Fishback's Florida upbringing, family relationships, driver's license, vehicle registration, voting history and work with Incubate Debate, a statewide nonprofit operating student debate programs throughout Florida. Collins' attorney Mark Meuser criticized the ruling and argued the court improperly accepted Fishback's explanation that he did not understand the legal significance of his Washington filings.

 Meuser did not indicate whether Collins plans to appeal the ruling. Unless an appellate court intervenes, Fishback will remain on the Aug. 18 Republican primary ballot alongside Collins, U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds and former House Speaker Paul Renner.

cards.headline: Cyclist rides through Vero Beach on 2,600-mile journey from Key West to Maine
cards.teaser: A Boston cyclist rode through Vero Beach this week on a 2,600-mile bike ride from Key West to Maine to honor a friend lost to colorectal cancer.
cards.body:

Weedall began his journey in Key West, pedaling 155 miles to Miami on day one. He set off on his second leg, a 163-mile ride to Vero Beach, after filling his hydration pack with ice to stay cool.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County families say Florida Medicaid abruptly cut autism therapy for children
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County parents say their children lost access to Applied Behavioral Analysis therapy after Medicaid abruptly stopped covering it. Florida's health agency has not explained why.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County parents say their children lost access to a critical autism therapy after Medicaid abruptly stopped covering it and Florida's health agency has not explained why. The therapy at the center of the dispute is Applied Behavioral Analysis, or ABA. The Cleveland Clinic describes it as a research-based behavior therapy for people with autism and other developmental disorders, adding that many studies have proven the effectiveness of ABA. Families connected to Reflection Services ABA Therapy in Lake Worth say they received notice that Medicaid would no longer cover their children's treatment.

 Daura Mabel Sanchez Cano de Fundora said her son David is classified by his neurologist as level one on the autism spectrum. She described the progress he had made through ABA, saying his vocabulary have been increasingly amazing and he can understand what is happening. Myrian Suarez, a mother of two boys with autism, said ABA gave her son tools to manage his emotions.

 Since the therapy stopped, Talia Quiroz said she has experienced dangerous regressions in her daughter's behavior. Suarez described similar physical consequences, saying she has bruised arms from one of her son's pinching.

 Reports of Medicaid cuts to ABA therapy have surfaced in states across the country. The Health and Human Services Office of the Inspector General audited Medicaid spending on ABA in Maine, Michigan, Wisconsin, and Colorado. Its findings identified roughly $200 million in what it considers improper payments among the four states.

 A separate audit in Nebraska found yearly Medicaid spending on ABA therapy multiplied 18 times over, across a five-year period. Questions were sent to Florida's Agency for Healthcare Administration, which runs the state's Medicaid program.

cards.headline: Florida congressman pushes bill requiring AI data centers to supply their own power and water
cards.teaser: Florida Republican U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds introduced legislation that would require hyperscale AI data centers to provide their own power generation and water resources instead of relying on public utilities.
cards.body:
Donalds introduced H.R. 9777, known as the Protecting Ratepayers Act, as the rapid expansion of hyperscale AI data centers raises concerns nationwide about strain on the power grid and water resources. The Electric Power Research Institute estimates data centers could consume up to 9% of all U.S. electricity generation by 2030, a sharp increase from current levels. Supporters of the proposal say it could help shield customers in Florida and across the country from future utility rate increases tied to growing energy demand from artificial intelligence infrastructure.

 The Trump administration recently announced the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, a voluntary agreement involving major technology companies, utilities and state leaders intended to keep the cost of powering new AI facilities from being passed on to residential and commercial utility customers. Donalds' legislation would move beyond voluntary commitments by creating federal requirements for large-scale AI data centers. The pledge has been signed by several major technology companies, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Oracle and xAI.

 Mehran Basiratmand, director of innovations and programs at Florida Atlantic University, said the proposed legislation could address some of the biggest public concerns surrounding AI data centers. Basiratmand previously served as chairperson of the policy board for what he described as the state's largest data center. He said requiring companies to generate their own power could encourage investment in alternative energy solutions rather than placing added pressure on public infrastructure.

hero.headline: Martin County Fire Chief warns homestead exemption could force station closures, firefighter layoffs
hero.body:
Martin County Fire Chief Chad Cianciulli warned Tuesday that a proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could force the closure of three fire stations, lay off 116 firefighters, and eliminate specialized emergency response teams. During the Martin County Commission meeting, Cianciulli presented a planning exercise showing the department's annual budget would decline by $9.5 million in the first year if voters approve the constitutional amendment in November. By the second year, the annual loss would reach $16.5 million, a 22% reduction from the current budget.

Under the scenario, Fire Rescue could close Station 18 on Britt Road, Station 33 in Hobe Sound, and Station 23 on Kanner Highway. The department could be forced to lay off as many as 116 firefighters by the second year, equivalent to one of the department's three shifts. The funding loss could force Martin County to eliminate specialized teams responsible for hazardous materials incidents, technical rescues and dive operations. The department could then have to request assistance from neighboring agencies in Palm Beach or St. Lucie counties, potentially increasing response times.

Cianciulli pointed to the deadly Camp Mystic flooding in Texas as an example of the delays that can occur when a community must rely on outside resources. "They had to call for outside assets, a 14-hour response to start mitigating that scene," Cianciulli said. "We're in a position in the county, if we have any incident here, we are able to do an immediate mitigation. We're not wasting any second." During public comment, one resident and a commissioner questioned whether reducing employee salaries could help address the potential shortfall.

Cianciulli responded that Martin County already has difficulty recruiting trained firefighter-paramedics because departments farther south offer better compensation. "When we did our last class that we had, we had roughly 22 open positions; I only had about three paramedics that actually graduated that class," Cianciulli said. "The rest were firefighter EMTs. It's because the compensation package for a firefighter medic that is already trained is much higher down south." Cianciulli advised residents to learn as much as possible about the proposal and its potential effects before casting their ballots in November.

cards.body:
The annual fundraiser allows guests to sample food, wine and beer from area businesses while participating restaurants compete for Big Taste awards and local bragging rights. Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties said the event helps fund mentorship opportunities for children who are currently waiting to be matched with a mentor, known as a Big.

 Community members can support the mission by purchasing tickets, attending the event or volunteering to become a mentor. Spritz Stuart plans to feature several menu items during the event promotion, including a Tuscan salmon dish, a smash burger and a specialty cocktail called the Fig & Flame.

 Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties serves children and families throughout Palm Beach and Martin counties through one-on-one mentoring relationships designed to support academic achievement, confidence and personal growth. Community events like Big Taste of Martin County continue to grow in popularity across South Florida as nonprofits look for new ways to connect residents with local causes while supporting area businesses and restaurants.

cards.headline: Indiantown Village Council rejects second attempt at data center pause
cards.teaser: Two Indiantown Village Council members failed to convince colleagues to approve a pause on data center applications, with the village attorney warning the move would violate state legislation.
cards.body:
Indiantown Village Councilwoman Karen Onsager moved that the Village of Indiantown establish a 90-day administrative pause on the acceptance, processing and approval of all new applications for large-load data center development projects during the July 13 budget workshop. The motion died after no council member offered a second. Onsager had requested the pause to allow the council and residents to better understand current and projected demands on water and electrical infrastructure through an informational meeting with technical experts, representatives from the South Florida Water Management District and utility providers.

 Village Attorney Wade Vose said such an administrative pause, whether 90 days or 12 months, would violate Senate Bill 180. Vose said he received an email that same afternoon from a local land use attorney who represents multiple developers within the Village, warning that SB 180 would prohibit anything along the lines of a regulation that would inhibit the process of applications for development. Mayor Carmine Dipaolo warned colleagues about offending state officials who have given the village over $120 million in funding.

 The council previously sought advice from Vose last month on a moratorium after scores of local residents protested the village's preliminary review of a data center application submitted by Nelson Ferreira, which he withdrew on April 29. Village Manager Taryn Kryzda confirmed the industrially zoned lands within the village allowed data centers as a permitted use. Onsager confirmed with Kryzda that a community meeting would be scheduled for Saturday, Aug. 2.

cards.headline: Martin County Fire Rescue could lose 116 firefighters under proposed property tax amendment
cards.teaser: Martin County commissioners are expected to hear a presentation Tuesday outlining how a proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could affect Martin County Fire Rescue i
cards.body:
Martin County commissioners are expected to hear a presentation Tuesday outlining how a proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could affect Martin County Fire Rescue if voters approve the constitutional amendment on the November ballot. According to county documents, Martin County Fire Rescue projects it could lose 116 firefighters over the next two years, about one-third of its workforce, because of reduced property tax revenue tied to the proposed amendment. Martin County Commissioner James Blake Capps said the county has been used to the very best in fire rescue services, and he would hate to see the level of service suffer greatly if the constitutional amendment passes.

 Fire Rescue leaders are expected to discuss potential operational changes if those revenue reductions occur. Previous county projections have outlined possible station closures, reductions to specialized teams including HAZMAT, Technical Rescue, the dive team and LifeStar, and delays in replacing equipment. County leaders have previously said the department has few options to absorb the projected revenue loss because about 93 percent of the Fire Rescue budget is dedicated to personnel. Officials have also warned the proposed cuts could lead to longer emergency response times and affect specialized emergency services provided throughout Martin County.

 Capps said there would also have to be a no-overtime policy for all fire rescue personnel, which would mean no backfilling of stations with personnel and would result in randomized brownouts of stations. He also warned that higher insurance premiums could result, noting that if you're within five miles of a fire station, you receive a break on your homeowner's insurance, but if you're farther than five miles away, you pay higher premiums. If the county shut down three fire stations, a lot of people would end up paying more for homeowner's insurance, Capps said.

 No vote on firefighter layoffs or fire station closures is expected during Tuesday's meeting. Instead, commissioners will receive the presentation as they continue evaluating the potential local impacts of the proposed homestead exemption expansion. Voters will have the final say on the constitutional amendment during the November general election. The meeting starts at 9 a.m.

cards.headline: Treasure Coast single-family home prices rise after two-year decline
cards.teaser: Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after drops from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St.
cards.body:
Single-family home prices are rising across the Treasure Coast after drops from 2023 to 2025. Martin County median home sale prices are up 1.1% since 2025, sitting at $655,000. St. Lucie County is seeing the highest increase in the region, up 2.3% since June 2025 with a median sale price of $399,000. Indian River County has seen an increase of 1.8%, with a median sales price of $400,000.

 Kelley Decowski, an award-winning realtor at REMAX in Stuart, said the increases are being driven by low supply and high demand. Decowski said buyers should start making decisions now because there are no signs that the prices are going to come back down. Inventory is low on the Treasure Coast, though the market is currently balanced for both buyers and sellers.

 Cara Collins, who bought her Martin County home before the COVID-19 pandemic when prices were significantly lower, said she has no plans to sell. Collins said current prices are higher than she would hope for, and that the market has changed what would be possible for her family today. She said she would not be able to be a stay-at-home mom and be able to afford a home for her kids if buying now.

 Condos and townhomes show different trends. Prices have dropped in Martin and St. Lucie counties and only increased by less than a percent in Indian River County. Decowski said buyers need to come in pre-approved before they go looking at homes, and sellers need to price their homes realistically and present a well-maintained product.
